content: Milk is a critical source of nutrition for children, particularly during their second year of life. At 12 months of age, children who are no longer breastfeeding are often introduced to animal milk, either full-fat or lower-fat, as a standard practice to support regular feeding and prevent undernutrition. Additionally, other types of milk, such as fortified milks enriched with extra nutrients, and plant-based milk alternatives, are available for children with lactose intolerance or allergies to human or cow’s milk proteins. Follow-on formulas marketed for children over one year of age are also used to partially meet nutritional requirements, although evidence supporting their benefits for young children is insufficient to recommend their use for optimal growth, health, and nutrition during this critical developmental period. The objective of this research was to evaluate the effects of animal milk consumption and its associated benefits or risks in children aged 12–23 months, compared to follow-on formulas, lower-fat milk, plant-based milk alternatives, or fortified milk. A comprehensive search was conducted in September 2020 across multiple databases, including CENTRAL, MEDLINE, Embase, and others, to identify relevant studies. Reference lists were reviewed, and authors and experts were contacted to identify additional studies with control groups. The inclusion criteria encompassed randomized controlled trials (RCTs) with individual or cluster randomization, non-randomized controlled trials, and comparative observational studies with control groups. Participants were healthy children aged 12–23 months, including those with low birth weight but without health conditions that could impede normal growth. The interventions compared included animal milk (full-fat or lower-fat) versus no milk, follow-on milk, plant-based milk, or fortified milk. Full-fat animal milk was also compared to lower-fat animal milk. Data collection and analysis involved two independent reviewers screening studies, extracting data, and assessing the risk of bias. Results were synthesized narratively, and meta-analyses were conducted for outcomes related to four intervention types. The certainty of effect estimates was assessed using the GRADE framework, categorized as very low, low, moderate, or high, and presented in evidence profile tables. The main results included 19 studies with 5,579 participants. Two studies were cluster-randomized, one RCT did not allow data extraction, and five studies contributed to qualitative analysis. The primary limitations of the studies were lack of blinding and selection bias. Most studies were conducted in highand middle-income countries, with eight funded by private industry and nine not reporting any declaration of interests. A single study compared animal milk (full-fat or lower-fat) to no other milk but did not allow data extraction, excluding it from the meta-analysis. Evidence from other studies suggested that daily consumption of 250 mL of cow’s milk in children aged 12–23 months increased the risk of insufficient intake of several nutrients, which could be mitigated by providing follow-on formula instead. While total energy and macronutrient intakes were similar between groups, protein intake in the cow’s milk group was significantly higher than recommended levels and higher than in children receiving follow-on formula. Two RCTs with non-randomized reference groups showed no beneficial effect of follow-on formula on children’s growth but a positive impact on hemoglobin concentrations. Feeding children aged 12–23 months with at least 250 mL of follow-on formula or fortified milk daily for 4–5 months demonstrated positive effects on anemia, hemoglobin levels, and improvements in vitamin D, serum iron, and zinc levels. However, follow-on formula or fortified milk may have similar effects to animal milk on growth, body composition, and child development, with little or no difference in the status of other nutrients. Milk is a vital food during childhood, providing energy, protein, calcium, phosphorus, and other micronutrients. Inappropriate feeding practices between 12 and 23 months of age can increase mortality and result in immediate and lifelong growth and developmental deficits. Breastfeeding remains the most appropriate liquid component of a progressively diversified diet for most children in this age group. However, many children are fed various types of milk or substitutes, including animal or plant-based milks, fortified milks, and follow-on formulas marketed for children over one year of age, often without proper justification of their benefits over appropriate dietary practices. The composition of milk is species-specific, designed to meet the nutritional needs of each species. Human milk, considered the gold standard, contains 9 g/L of protein compared to 34 g/L in cow’s milk, with higher lactose content in human milk (70 g/L vs. 48 g/L in cow’s milk). Fat content is similar, but cow’s milk has significantly higher saturated fatty acids. Human milk protein is dominated by the whey fraction (60%), while casein constitutes 40%. Immunoglobulin A (IgA) is the major immunoglobulin in human milk, higher than in other species. Animal milk, particularly cow’s milk, has traditionally been the first choice for regular feeding when young children are not breastfed. It is a rich and affordable source of protein, calcium, and vitamin D, supporting linear growth due to its potassium, magnesium, phosphorus, zinc, and high lactose content, which enhances mineral absorption. However, unmodified cow’s milk negatively impacts iron status, making it a strong determinant of iron deficiency. Low-fat milk refers to animal milk with reduced fat content (75–99.5% fat reduction). Reduced-fat milk has a high percentage of energy from protein (28% in 2% milk and 39% in skimmed milk), which is why it is not typically recommended for infants and young children. Skimmed milk is not suitable as a major food source for children under two years due to its lack of essential fatty acids, fat-soluble vitamins, and high renal solute load relative to energy. Semi-skimmed milk may be acceptable after 12 months of age. Follow-on formulas are milkor plant protein-based formulas designed to partially meet the nutritional needs of children aged 1–3 years. They can increase the supply of certain micronutrients in this age group. However, follow-on formulas marketed for children over one year often replace breastfeeding and are classified as breast milk substitutes. Despite supplementation with essential nutrients, many formulas differ significantly in composition compared to human milk. Plant-based formulas, such as those derived from soy or rice hydrolysates, are alternatives for children with lactose intolerance or allergies to human or cow’s milk proteins. While earlier versions had nutritional deficiencies, current soy formulas are supplemented with amino acids (e.g., methionine, taurine, carnitine) and minerals (e.g., iron, zinc, calcium, phosphorus). Concerns remain about potential hormonal effects on the reproductive system due to isoflavones in soy protein. Fortified milk contains additional nutrients not naturally present in significant amounts and is not necessarily marketed to infants and children. It is a complementary feeding option, addressing specific nutrient deficiencies in young children.
